To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) biofilms of filamentous cyanbacteria strongly induce calcite precipitation by photosynthesis, but inhibit precipitation in the dark; (2) the photosynthesis-induced calcification is not reflected in bulk stable isotope records of the calcified biofilms; and (3) syntaxial overgrowth by microspar is a result of photosynthesis-induced calcificaiton.

1) photosynthesis-induced CaCO3 precipitated in the biofilm but did not leave a stable isotopic imprint in the tufa; 2) the tufa fabric reflects the temperature-dependent diffusion coefficient of Ca2+ and HCO3−; 3) the annual laminations are not a reliable indicator of the annual growth rate; and 4) the sheath encrustation is not a reliable indicator for photosynthesis-induced precipitation.

The main takeaway from our work is that
photosynthesis can induce CaCO3 precipitation in the absence of a detectable signal in the water chemistry or in the stable isotope record of the precipitated carbonate.
microbial photosynthesis and respiration have significant impact on CaCO3 deposition in biofilms and tufas, but this effect may not be recorded in bulk water chemistry and stable isotopic records.
the microbial control of calcite precipitation and the resulting fabric formation of the biofilms are highly dependent on environmental factors and the specific microbial community.
